call.title: Live Trading Session — Rapid Setup Scan, AAPL & DELL Options

rules.rule: Trading is about finding the best available setup, not being perfect — a rule you can't hit 100% of the time isn't the point.
rules.why: Trying to protect a perfect record means you'll never really trade; the job is a system run over and over, not perfection.
rules.scope: General trading mindset — not instrument-specific, applies across whatever he's trading.

rules.rule: On a small/new account, once you're up meaningfully (he used 1% today), trim — sell part of the position rather than risk giving the gain back.
rules.why: Growing a new account means not sitting there taking a bunch of risk once you already have a win in hand.
rules.scope: !! SCOPE LIMIT: 2026 stock options (this call, 27 Aug and 3 Sep) — a percentage-of-account trim rule, not a dollar figure or a futures rule. Do not carry to ES futures or to the April 2024 20%-cap/2-5-10 ladder.

rules.rule: Default strike is at-the-money. You can go up to two strikes out-of-the-money only if you are actively in front of the computer and can manage the trade; if you might step away (errand, lunch, a meeting), stay at-the-money.
rules.why: Being away from the screen with a wider strike risks a bad position you can't react to — you want freedom to move around during the day.
rules.scope: !! SCOPE LIMIT: 2026 stock options sizing (this call, 27 Aug, 3 Sep). This is a DIFFERENT convention from the April 2024 options ladder (2/5/10 contracts, 20% account cap) — do not merge the two, and do not carry either to ES futures.

rules.rule: The stop/exit rule he actually uses on these options trades: watch the candle you entered on — if price closes back through that candle's open (against you), get out.
rules.why: No candle runs perfectly straight up or down — this gives an objective point to exit rather than reacting to P&L.
rules.scope: !! SCOPE LIMIT: Stated as “what I do” on his own 2026 stock-options day trades (AAPL/DELL here) — not phrased as an instruction Josh must follow, and never stated for ES futures. This is the first time in the corpus Jason has given ANY stop rule of his own (as opposed to Lige's stock-chart moving-average stops from Nov 2025) — see questions.

rules.rule: A secondary exit condition: if the stock makes a new high, pulls back, and tests the prior day's low without bouncing, get out of the trade.
rules.why: That failure to bounce off yesterday's low is read as the trade no longer working.
rules.scope: !! SCOPE LIMIT: same 2026 stock-options frame as the rule above; not stated for futures.

rules.rule: A conditional add-on: if price instead bounces off yesterday's high and you're down roughly 20% on the position, you can add another contract — then even a bounce that doesn't make a new high can put you back in profit.
rules.why: Averaging into a bounce off a known level, rather than an arbitrary price.
rules.scope: !! SCOPE LIMIT: same 2026 stock-options frame; a specific conditional add-on, not a general permission to average down.

rules.rule: Never chase a fill you missed — if your limit order doesn't fill at your price, let it go rather than jumping in at a worse price.
rules.why: Chasing turns a missed entry into a worse one.

rules.rule: Don't manage too many open positions at once — close one out before adding much else so your attention isn't scattered.
rules.why: Focus on one thing at a time rather than juggling multiple orders.

rules.rule: Always check the higher time frame (weekly/daily) to confirm the lower time frame before treating a level as real.
rules.why: The higher time frame is what confirms whether the lower time frame's level actually holds.

rules.rule: Gap rules apply in both directions — an unfilled gap matters whether price gapped up or down.
These aren't hardline, set-in-stone rules — read the context of the day rather than applying them mechanically.
rules.why: Treating them as rigid rules is what makes a trader inflexible; every day the market behaves differently.

setups.name: Top-wick reclaim
setups.trigger: Price pushing up toward a prior high's wick, at-the-money strike, decent volume/open interest.
setups.invalidation: Price doesn't reach the wick — "probably gonna bounce."

setups.name: No-follow-through rejection (avoid)
setups.trigger: Not a buy setup as-is. Re-entry requires either a break above the resistance/order block with a new high, or a pullback to retest support for a better price.
setups.invalidation: Continues to reject at resistance with no follow-through — stay out.

setups.name: Downtrend break needs a resistance retest, not an immediate entry
setups.trigger: An actual test of the resistance line that holds (not a brief touch — he called a weak touch “weak sauce”) opens a scalp on the rejection.
setups.invalidation: A touch that doesn't really hit the level isn't a signal yet.
setups.timeframe: weekly for the level, scalp on a lower time frame

setups.name: Beaten-down name holding major weekly support
setups.trigger: A move above a round-number level (here $20 on RGTI) is what turns this into a longer swing, not a scalp.
setups.invalidation: A break below the support level (he named $14 on RGTI) with a new low means remove it from the watch list.

setups.name: Round-number resistance breakout
setups.trigger: A clean break above a round-number resistance level (traders cluster orders at round numbers) with room to the next round number as target.

setups.name: Downtrend-break watch, breakout vs. dead-cat-bounce
setups.trigger: Break above the drawn resistance line targets the next round number up.
setups.invalidation: Failing to break — he called it a possible “dead cat bounce” back toward the lower level.

setups.name: The DELL trade: trend-line break entry, end-of-day candle stop
setups.trigger: Price breaking the drawn trend line to the upside on the intraday chart, entered near the break with a limit order; target was the $600 round number on the underlying.
setups.invalidation: End of day, no new high made — the entry candle's open got taken out on the pullback, so the position was cut for a small loss rather than held into the weekly contract's decay.

glossary.plain: The thin line above or below a candle's body showing the high or low price briefly touched but not held.
glossary.said: trying to tip over here to this top of the wick

glossary.plain: An option whose strike price is the same as (or closest to) the stock's current price.
glossary.said: What option do I want to trade? At the money, right?

glossary.plain: The total number of a specific option contract currently held open by traders — higher OI generally means more liquidity.
glossary.said: Look at the volume on this. Look at the open interest.

glossary.plain: How much an option's price is expected to move for a $1 move in the stock; also loosely used as the rough odds the option finishes in-the-money.
glossary.said: I want at least to have a 30 delta.

glossary.plain: A cluster of price action (often a big candle or consolidation) that acted as major buying or selling pressure, and tends to act as support/resistance later.
glossary.said: Because it's a big order block right on the top of it.

glossary.plain: Continued movement in the same direction after an initial move or breakout — its absence is a warning sign.
glossary.said: There's no follow through.

glossary.plain: A two-candle reversal pattern where a bullish candle fully ‘engulfs’ the prior bearish candle's body, often read as a reversal signal.
glossary.said: Is that a bullish engulfing? Yes.

glossary.plain: Volume-Weighted Average Price — the average price a stock has traded at today, weighted by volume; often used as an intraday support/resistance reference.
glossary.said: Just look for it to come off a VWAP.

glossary.plain: A jump in price between one candle's close and the next candle's open with no trading in between; a ‘gap fill’ is price later trading back through that empty zone.
glossary.said: So gap rules are in effect. So far, it's not filled the gap either way.

glossary.plain: A scalp is a quick, small in-and-out trade taken the same session; a swing is a position held for days or longer.
glossary.said: Do I want to swing it? No.

glossary.plain: The rate an option's price decays each day purely from time passing, holding everything else equal.
glossary.said: I'm going to lose how much on theta?

glossary.plain: An options position that combines buying and selling different contracts on the same underlying to define risk, rather than holding a single naked call or put.
glossary.said: Unless you're doing a spread trade, which you're not doing yet.

glossary.plain: A measure of how much a stock tends to move relative to its index — a beta above 1 means it typically moves more than the index.
glossary.said: Then you look at their beta.

glossary.plain: A short-lived bounce in a stock that's still in a broader downtrend, which often fails and rolls back over.
glossary.said: It's just a dead cap bounce and could come all the way back to 220.

glossary.plain: A rebound in price after a widely-feared event turns out less bad than expected — the fear was priced in, so the market bounces once it passes.
glossary.said: So this is what they call a relief rally.

glossary.plain: A scheduled event with a genuinely uncertain, all-or-nothing-style outcome (a Fed decision, earnings, a jobs report) that can move price sharply either way.
glossary.said: Anytime you have a binary event.

glossary.plain: Buying an option whose strike is two increments away from at-the-money, rather than exactly at-the-money.
glossary.said: You can go two strikes out.

glossary.plain: Selling part (not all) of a position to lock in some profit while keeping the rest on.
glossary.said: Normally when I trim, I just get out of position.

glossary.plain: A third-party options-flow tracking tool (and one of its features, “Market Tide”) that shows where large options premium is flowing across the market.
glossary.said: I'm gonna take a look at unusual whales real quick.

glossary.plain: The market's expectation of how much a stock will move, priced into an option's premium — higher IV means a more expensive option for the same strike.
glossary.said: Apply volatility 60.

insights.title: Pattern recognition has to be fast, not slow
insights.body: He deliberately scans charts at high speed during the call because traders need to recognize setups quickly, not deliberate for minutes — he compares it to reflexes in a video game and says slow thinking leads nowhere.
insights.said: Traders are not slow in their brain; they're quick.

insights.title: The market always gives you another chance
insights.body: You don't have to force a decision on a trade going the wrong way, because the market tends to offer another entry later — so there's no need to either take a loss prematurely or stubbornly hold a losing position.
insights.said: They're going to give me a chance even if it's just here.

insights.title: Don't be schizophrenic about a trade
insights.body: Your reason for being in a trade is the setup, not the day's P&L swings — if the chart hasn't actually changed, your conviction shouldn't flip just because you're briefly down.

insights.title: Perfectionism is the enemy of a working system
insights.body: Trading is systematic, not about being right every time; trying to protect a perfect record means avoiding real trades altogether. He ties this to a biblical framing (losing your life to save it) to argue that clinging to perfection guarantees you never really trade.
insights.said: It's not about perfection. It's about reading a setup and finding the best one that's available.

insights.title: 70% of an individual stock's move comes from its index
insights.body: Because most of a stock's daily movement is explained by the index it belongs to (S&P 500 / Nasdaq), trading names inside a reliable index is safer than micro-caps or small-caps outside one — and beta tells you how much more or less a name moves than its index.
insights.said: 70% of any individual stock's move is based on the index that it's involved in.

insights.title: Context is king — these aren't hardline rules
insights.body: Treating every rule as fixed and mechanical makes a trader inflexible. Some days the market goes sideways, some days straight up or down for no clear reason, so judgment has to adapt to conditions rather than follow a rigid checklist.
insights.said: You need context with some of these. These aren't like hardline rules.

insights.title: Fear of failing (not the market) is what wrecks decision-making
insights.body: He connects Josh's perfectionism directly to fear — worrying that his mentor or his dad will be disappointed if he's not perfect — and says that fear, not the market itself, is what causes bad trading decisions.
insights.said: Because you weren't perfect... and that's what's happened to you in your trading.

insights.title: Managing a small/new account means playing defense on gains, not swinging for a home run
insights.body: With a small account, the discipline is to take a small, consistent win (he used 1% today), lock part of it in, and compound rather than chase a big single trade — the home runs come naturally once you're consistent, not by reaching for them.
insights.said: Start off with small goals and celebrate the small wins.

insights.title: Go looking for the opportunity every day, expecting to find one
insights.body: His personal approach is to start each day assuming there's a good trade to find (a 'treasure hunt'), rather than waiting passively — he frames this as trusting that an opportunity is out there rather than needing certainty upfront.
insights.said: I wake up in the morning, I'm like God, where I want a treasure hunt?

insights.title: A missed fill is a missed fill — chasing it turns a good process into a bad trade
insights.body: Even when a trade goes on to work without you, chasing the entry after the fact (rather than accepting you didn't get filled at your price) is what turns a disciplined process into an emotional one.
insights.said: If I don't get it, I'm not chasing it.
